cues.text: Let us now look at some additional examples of data-driven decisions, and in particular at the full process that turns raw data into a sound business decision.
Start with the process itself.
The full decision process begins with a specific business need and a success criterion.
That order matters.
Before anyone opens a spreadsheet or a database, the organisation must say what problem it is trying to solve and how it will recognise success.
Without that, data collection becomes aimless.
Next, you gather relevant data, both internal and external.
Internal data might be sales records or customer transactions held by the firm.
External data might come from market reports or other outside sources.
Then you validate that data for completeness and provenance.
Completeness asks whether anything is missing.
Provenance asks where the data came from and whether that source can be trusted.
After validation, you clean and transform the data, so that it is in a usable form.
Then you choose an analytical method suited to the question.
Once you have results, you interpret them in context, because a number means little without the business situation around it.
You then communicate your findings through reports and visuals, so that decision makers can understand them.
After that, you implement a decision, and finally you monitor the outcome to see whether the decision actually delivered what was intended.
Throughout every one of these steps, alignment with strategy is required.
At each stage, you ask whether the work still serves the organisation's strategic direction.
Now, the tools.
Different tools suit different tasks, and it helps to keep the distinctions clear.
Excel and Google Sheets support small-scale exploration.
They are ideal when you are looking at a modest amount of data and want to explore it quickly.
SQL and database management systems, or DBMSs, support structured querying.
That means asking precise questions of data stored in organised tables.
SPSS and R support statistical analysis.
Python supports processing, modelling and automation, so it can prepare data, build models and automate repeated work.
Power BI and Tableau support interactive reporting, letting users explore dashboards and visuals.
Hadoop and Spark support distributed workloads, where the data or the computation is spread across many machines.
The key lesson is this: choosing a tool depends on the task and the scale, not on prestige.
A famous tool is not automatically the right one.
Now let us turn to examples.
The lecture illustrates three well-known cases.
First, Amazon's personalisation and logistics: data is used to tailor what customers see, and to support how goods are stored and delivered.
Second, Netflix's data-informed content and recommendation decisions: data informs both what content is offered and what is recommended to viewers.
Third, Tesco's loyalty-data segmentation: data from a loyalty scheme is used to divide customers into meaningful groups.
Remember that these are lecture examples that illustrate the ideas.
They are not, by themselves, a statistical proof.
Other applications include dynamic pricing, revenue management, competitor analysis, new service discovery and fraud-risk monitoring.
Take dynamic pricing.
Dynamic prices can reflect demand and inventory, so prices may move as demand rises or stock changes.
But such pricing should be transparent, legally compliant, and tested for discriminatory or exploitative effects.
A price that is efficient for the firm may still be unfair to customers, so it must be checked.
Next, data quality.
Data quality has several dimensions: accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity and uniqueness.
Accuracy asks whether values are correct.
Completeness asks whether required data is present.
Consistency asks whether the data agrees across systems.
Timeliness asks whether it is up to date.
Validity asks whether it follows the required formats and rules.
Uniqueness asks whether each item appears only once.
Here is why this matters.
Imagine a business intelligence warehouse that holds duplicate sales records.
Those duplicates can inflate revenue, regardless of how good the dashboard quality is.
A beautiful dashboard built on faulty data simply presents wrong numbers beautifully.
To protect against this, you establish ownership, so someone is accountable for the data.
You establish data lineage, so you can trace where data came from and how it changed.
You set validation rules, access permissions and monitoring.
One more important distinction: correlation, prediction and causal evidence are different things.
Two measures moving together is correlation.
A model that anticipates future values is prediction.
Causal evidence shows that one thing actually produces another.
A forecast alone cannot establish that a proposed intervention will work.
Predicting that sales will fall is not the same as knowing that a specific action will fix it.
Finally, a worked decision.
Suppose sales fall while inventory availability also falls.
The association suggests stockouts, meaning customers cannot buy items because they are not in stock.
But be careful.
Promotions, seasonality and pricing may also explain the fall in sales.
So the analyst compares relevant periods and products, to see whether the pattern holds consistently.
The analyst investigates missing stock, to confirm where and why items were unavailable.
Then the business pilots a replenishment intervention, trying a restocking approach on a limited basis first.
And it measures margin and waste as well as availability.
This matters because restocking could raise availability while hurting profit margin or creating waste, for example through excess stock.
Notice what this example is.
It is a decision process, not merely a descriptive dashboard.
A dashboard might show that sales and availability both fell.
The decision process goes further: it tests explanations, trials an action, and measures the wider consequences.
